concepts.name: Proto-Shiva / Pashupati Seal: Identity and Interpretation
key_dimensions: Description of the seal — seated figure in yogic posture surrounded by animals (elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo, deer)
Debate: Whether the figure truly represents proto-Shiva or an unrelated deity — Marshall vs. later scholars like Asko Parpola
Significance as possible precursor to Shaiva tradition and concept of 'Lord of Animals'
UPSC trap: The seal is from Mohenjo-daro, NOT Harappa — common location confusion

concepts.name: Mother Goddess Figurines: Nature and Religious Significance
key_dimensions: Terracotta female figurines found abundantly — interpreted as fertility cult or Mother Goddess worship
Comparison with similar figurines in Mesopotamian and Egyptian civilisations — shared fertility symbolism
Debate: Whether these represent a goddess or were merely toys/decorative objects (Kenoyer's counter-view)
UPSC trap: Male figurines also exist but are far fewer — questions on 'which type dominated' are common

concepts.name: Tree and Nature Worship: Sacred Pipal and Animal Veneration
key_dimensions: Pipal (Ficus religiosa) tree depicted on seals and tablets — considered sacred, possible continuity to later Hindu/Buddhist traditions
Animals like humped bull (zebu), unicorn, and composite creatures on seals — possible totemic or religious significance
Distinction: Pipal worship as evidence of nature religion vs. later Vedic fire-altar religion
UPSC trap: The 'unicorn' is the MOST commonly depicted animal on IVC seals — not the bull as often assumed

concepts.name: Fire Altars at Kalibangan and Lothal: Evidence of Fire Worship
key_dimensions: Fire altars (havankundas) discovered at Kalibangan — rows of fire altars in the lower town citadel area
Similar fire pit evidence at Lothal — debated whether ritual or domestic/industrial use
Significance: Possible proto-Vedic fire worship ritual or ancestor of yajna tradition
UPSC trap: Fire altars are at Kalibangan (most confirmed), NOT universally found at all IVC sites — do not generalise

concepts.name: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro: Ritual Purification Hypothesis
key_dimensions: Structure: Brick-lined tank (~12m x 7m), watertight with bitumen, surrounded by galleries and rooms
Dominant interpretation: Ritual bathing/purification — possible precursor to temple tank traditions
Counter-interpretations: Public bathing facility, administrative use, or seasonal water storage
UPSC trap: The Great Bath is on the CITADEL mound, not the lower town — and is unique to Mohenjo-daro among major sites

concepts.name: Unicorn Seal and Its Religious-Cultic Significance
key_dimensions: Unicorn (one-horned bull) is the most frequently depicted motif on IVC seals
Object in front of unicorn interpreted as a 'ritual offering stand' or 'filter/incense burner' — religious paraphernalia
Parpola's interpretation: Unicorn linked to a specific clan or deity in a polytheistic system
UPSC trap: 'Unicorn' in IVC context is a one-horned bull figure — not a horse-like creature as in Western mythology

concepts.name: Burial Practices and Afterlife Beliefs in IVC
key_dimensions: Primary burial (extended inhumation) most common — body laid in brick-lined graves with grave goods (pottery, ornaments)
Evidence of fractional burial and urn burial at some sites (Harappa, Lothal) — suggesting varied beliefs
Grave goods imply belief in afterlife — continuity of individual identity post-death
UPSC trap: Unlike Egyptians, IVC people did NOT practice mummification — and large-scale monumental tombs are ABSENT

concepts.name: Absence of Temples: Implications for Understanding IVC Religion
key_dimensions: No structure conclusively identified as a temple in any major IVC site — unlike Mesopotamia or Egypt
Possible domestic shrines inferred from figurines found in houses
Scholarly debate: Was religion decentralised/household-based, or did public structures like the Great Bath serve ritual purposes?
UPSC trap: Absence of temples does NOT mean absence of religion — a nuanced point frequently tested in mains

concepts.name: Linga and Yoni Symbols: Proto-Shaiva Continuity Debate
key_dimensions: Stone objects interpreted as proto-lingas (cylindrical stones) and ring stones (ring-shaped, interpreted as yoni) found at IVC sites
Marshall's argument: Direct continuity with later Shaiva phallic worship tradition
Counter-view (Shereen Ratnagar, Kenoyer): These may be gaming pieces, weights, or architectural elements — not necessarily religious
UPSC trap: The continuity thesis between IVC and Hinduism is a contested scholarly position, NOT an established fact

concepts.name: Composite and Mythical Creatures on Seals: Religious Iconography
key_dimensions: Seals depict multi-headed animals, part-human part-animal figures — suggesting mythological narratives
Interpreted as evidence of a complex mythology similar to Mesopotamian religious iconography
Possible connection to later Puranic traditions of vahanas (divine mounts) and composite divine beings
UPSC trap: Composite creatures appear on seals, NOT in sculpture — medium specificity is frequently tested

concepts.name: Water and Drainage System as Ritual vs. Civic Infrastructure
key_dimensions: Elaborate drainage at Mohenjo-daro interpreted by some as religiously motivated ritual purity concerns
Alternative view: Purely functional civic planning with no ritual significance
Comparison: Contrast with later Hindu concepts of ritual purity (achara/shaucha) — possible continuity
UPSC trap: The drainage system is urban infrastructure — attributing it solely to ritual purity is an interpretive leap, not confirmed fact

concepts.name: Indus Script and Its Possible Religious Content
key_dimensions: Script remains undeciphered — over 400 signs identified, mostly on seals
Hypothesis: Seals may have served as amulets, priestly insignia, or votive objects with religious inscriptions
Parpola's attempt to link script to proto-Dravidian language with Vedic/ritual connotations
UPSC trap: The script is NOT bilingual (no Rosetta Stone equivalent) and has NOT been deciphered — questions test awareness of this limitation

concepts.name: Evidence of Sacrifice: Animal and Possible Human
key_dimensions: Animal bones in fire altars at Kalibangan suggest possible animal sacrifice rituals
Debated evidence of human sacrifice — mass graves at Mohenjo-daro (the 'massacre' layer) now largely re-interpreted as plague/disease deaths
Comparison with contemporary Bronze Age civilisations where sacrifice is documented
UPSC trap: Human sacrifice in IVC is NOT proven — the massacre skeletons have multiple competing explanations

concepts.name: Amulets, Seals as Votive/Apotropaic Objects
key_dimensions: Small terracotta and faience amulets found widely — suggest protection magic and apotropaic religious practices
Seals possibly worn as amulets or used in ritual exchange, not merely commercial purposes
Miniature tablets with repeated iconography suggest standardised religious symbolism across urban centres
UPSC trap: Seals had DUAL function (commercial + possible ritual) — single-function interpretations are considered reductive

concepts.name: Yoga and Meditative Postures in IVC Iconography
key_dimensions: Pashupati seal figure in a cross-legged, possibly meditative posture — cited as earliest evidence of yoga
Other seated figurines in similar postures found at multiple sites
Debate: Is this genuine proto-yoga or simply a culturally common seated posture? (Position of Marshall vs. modern yoga historians)
UPSC trap: IVC as 'origin of yoga' is a popular but contested claim — UPSC may test the nuance between iconographic inference and historical proof

concepts.name: Continuity vs. Discontinuity: IVC Religion and Later Hinduism
key_dimensions: Continuity argument: Mother Goddess, Shiva prototype, tree worship, ritual bathing, linga-yoni all have Hindu parallels
Discontinuity argument: No Vedic fire sacrifice (yajna), no soma ritual evidence, no devas — suggesting these are separate traditions
Synthesis view (Romila Thapar): Selective cultural absorption occurred during post-IVC period
UPSC trap: UPSC frequently tests whether students confuse 'similarity' with 'continuity' — these are methodologically different claims

concepts.name: Regional Variation in Religious Practices Across IVC Sites
key_dimensions: Fire altars specific to Kalibangan; Great Bath unique to Mohenjo-daro; cemetery diversity at Harappa — suggests regional religious variation
Absence of uniform religious iconography across all sites challenges monolithic interpretation of IVC religion
Implication: IVC may have been religiously pluralistic — different communities with different cults
UPSC trap: Students often treat IVC religion as homogeneous — site-specific religious evidence is a high-yield differentiation topic

concepts.name: Dancing Girl Bronze Statue: Secular or Religious Artefact?
key_dimensions: Bronze lost-wax (cire perdue) cast figurine from Mohenjo-daro — depicts a young woman in a confident pose
Interpretations range from a temple dancer (devadasi precursor), to a secular artistic depiction, to a deity
Significance of the casting technique — indicates advanced metallurgical knowledge independent of religious context
UPSC trap: The Dancing Girl is from Mohenjo-daro, NOT Harappa — and its religious attribution is interpretive, not confirmed

concepts.name: Swastika and Other Symbols: Religious Iconography on IVC Artefacts
key_dimensions: Swastika symbol found on IVC pottery and seals — one of earliest known uses of this symbol
Interpreted as a solar symbol, good-luck charm, or ritual motif — predates its later use in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism
Cross-cultural parallel: Same symbol found in Mesopotamia, ancient Europe — raises question of independent invention vs. diffusion
UPSC trap: IVC swastika is among the OLDEST known examples globally — its later Hindu religious meaning should not be retroactively applied
